nameStory: The 'cleft-leaved' part of this hawthorn's name comes from its deeply divided leaves that look like they've been split or cleft with a knife. The word 'cleft' means split or divided, perfectly describing how this tree's leaves are cut into distinct lobes that separate them from other hawthorns.
description: Cleft-leaved hawthorn is a small, thorny tree or large shrub that typically grows 10-20 feet tall. Like other hawthorns, it's armed with sharp thorns along its branches and produces clusters of white flowers in spring followed by small red fruits. What sets this species apart is its distinctive deeply lobed leaves that are more dramatically divided than most of its hawthorn relatives. It's quite rare in New England, making it a special find for plant enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cleft leaves with 5-7 sharp, pointed lobes that cut more than halfway to the midrib, giving them an almost hand-like appearance. The lobes feel thin and papery when mature, with a smooth texture on top.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White, 5-petaled flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters of 5-12 blooms in late spring. Each flower is about half an inch across with a sweet, honey-like fragrance and numerous pink-tipped stamens.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small red berries (called pomes) about 1/4 inch across that ripen in late summer. They feel firm and contain 2-5 hard seeds, with flesh that tastes somewhat dry and mealy.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Sharp, straight thorns up to 2 inches long scattered along the branches. They're hard and woody, capable of easily piercing skin, so handle with care.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that becomes scaly and furrowed with age. On young branches, the bark feels smooth and has a reddish-brown tint.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small, dense tree or large shrub with an irregular, often multi-stemmed crown. Branches tend to zigzag slightly and create a somewhat thorny, impenetrable thicket when mature.

habitat: Cleft-leaved hawthorn prefers sunny, open areas with well-drained soils, often found along woodland edges, old fields, and rocky slopes. In New England, it's typically discovered in areas with limestone or calcareous soils, particularly in valleys and lower elevations. Given its rarity in the region, it's most likely to be encountered in southern New England where conditions are more favorable.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in early May, followed by showy white flower clusters in late May to early June that attract bees and other pollinators with their sweet scent.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed out with the distinctive deeply cleft leaves most visible, while small green fruits begin developing and gradually enlarge through the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange-red before dropping, and the bright red fruits ripen and become most noticeable against the autumn landscape.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the zigzag branching pattern and prominent thorns, while some dried fruits may persist, and gray scaly bark becomes a key identification feature.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare in New England with only 7 recorded observations, cleft-leaved hawthorn can live for over 100 years and was once used by Native Americans to make extremely strong bows because hawthorn wood is nearly as hard as oak but much more flexible.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other hawthorns, but the deeply cleft leaves that are cut more than halfway to the midrib distinguish it from species like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn which have shallower lobes. Remember: if the leaf looks like it was cut with scissors almost to the center vein, you might have found this rare species.
contextualKnowledge: Hawthorns are notoriously difficult to identify even for experts because there are so many similar species that can hybridize with each other. The Crataegus genus is considered one of the most taxonomically challenging plant groups in North America, with some botanists recognizing over 1,000 species while others argue for far fewer distinct species.
compareHints: Cleft-leaved hawthorn's leaves are much more deeply divided than most New England hawthorns - while dotted hawthorn has shallow lobes and cockspur hawthorn has barely any lobes at all, this species' leaves are cut nearly to the midrib. Fanleaf hawthorn has similarly deep cuts, but its lobes are broader and more fan-shaped rather than narrow and pointed. The combination of very deep, narrow leaf lobes makes this species distinctive within the challenging hawthorn group.
